etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English pryde, pride, from Old English prȳde, prȳte (“pride”) (compare Old Norse prýði (“bravery, pomp”)), derivative of Old English prūd (“proud”). More at proud. The verb derives from the noun, at least since the 12th century.

definitions.definition: The quality or state of being proud; an unreasonable overestimation of one's own superiority in terms of talents, looks, wealth, importance etc., which comes across as being lofty, distant, and often showing contempt of others.
(having a positive sense, often with of or in) A sense of one's own worth, and scorn for what is beneath or unworthy of oneself.

quote.citation: 1766, Oliver Goldsmith, chapter 3, in The Vicar of Wakefield:
quote.text: My chief attention therefore was now to bring down the pride of my family to their circumstances; for I well knew that aspiring beggary is wretchedness itself.

quote.citation: 1849–1861, Thomas Babington Macaulay, chapter XII, in The History of England from the Accession of James the Second, volume (please specify |volume=I to V), London: Longman, Brown, Green, and Longmans, →OCLC:
quote.text: A people which takes no pride in the noble achievements of remote ancestors will never achieve anything worthy to be remembered with pride by remote descendants.

quote.citation: 1790-1793, William Blake, The Marriage of Heaven and Hell
quote.text: The pride of the peacock is the glory of God.

definitions.definition: Proud or disdainful behavior or treatment; insolence or arrogance of demeanor; haughty bearing and conduct; insolent exultation.

quote.citation: 1912, G. K. Chesterton, Introduction to Aesop's Fables:

definitions.definition: That of which one is proud; that which excites boasting or self-congratulation; the occasion or ground of self-esteem, or of arrogant and presumptuous confidence, as beauty, ornament, noble character, children, etc.

quote.citation: 1590, Edmund Spenser, “(please specify the book)”, in The Faerie Queene. […], London:  […]  [John Wolfe] for William Ponsonbie, →OCLC:
quote.text: lofty trees yclad with summer's pride

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Zechariah 9:6:
quote.text: And a bastard shall dwell in Ashdod, and I will cut off the pride of the Philistines.

quote.citation: 1770, [Oliver] Goldsmith, The Deserted Village, a Poem, London:  […]  W[illiam] Griffin, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: a bold peasantry, their country's pride

quote.citation: c. 1603–1604 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of Othello, the Moore of Venice”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act III, scene iii]:
quote.text: Pride, pomp and circumstance of glorious war.

definitions.definition: Highest pitch; elevation reached; loftiness; prime; glory.

quote.citation: c. 1606 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of Macbeth”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act II, scene iv]:
quote.text: a falcon, towering in her pride of place

definitions.definition: Consciousness of power; fullness of animal spirits; mettle; wantonness.
Lust; sexual desire; especially, excitement of sexual appetite in a female animal.
(zoology, collective) A company of lions or other large felines.
Alternative letter-case form of Pride (“festival for LGBT people”).
(reflexive) To take or experience pride in something; to be proud of it.

quote.citation: 1820, Washington Irving, The Legend of Sleepy Hollow:
quote.text: Ichabod prided himself upon his dancing as much as upon his vocal powers. Not a limb, not a fibre about him was idle; and to have seen his loosely hung frame in full motion and clattering about the room you would have thought Saint Vitus himself, that blessed patron of the dance, was figuring before you in person.

quote.citation: 2021 December 29, Paul Stephen, “Rail's accident investigators”, in RAIL, number 947, page 32:
quote.text: RAIB prides itself on being able to send any of its inspectors to site with sufficient investigative skills and technical knowledge to gather evidence for any type of accident.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English pryde, from Middle Low German lampride, from Medieval Latin lampreda.

definitions.definition: (zoology) The small European lamprey species Petromyzon branchialis.
